No. _______
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
MARKWAYNE MULLIN, ET AL., APPLICANTS
v.
FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH, ET AL.
───────────
APPLICATION FOR A STAY OF THE INJUNCTION
ISSUED BY THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE WESTERN DISTRICT OF TEXAS
───────────
D. JOHN SAUER
   Solicitor General
      Counsel of Record
   Department of Justice
   Washington, D.C. 20530-0001
   SupremeCtBriefs@usdoj.gov
   (202) 514-2217

ii
PARTIES TO THE PROCEEDING
Applicants (defendants below) are Markwayne Mullin, in his official capacity
as Secretary of Homeland Security; the U.S. Department of Homeland Security; and
U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
Respondents (plaintiffs below) are Friends of the Ruidosa Church; Center for
Biological Diversity; and Danny William Miller Junior.
RELATED PROCEEDINGS
United States District Court (W.D. Tex.):
Friends of the Ruidosa Church v. Mullin, No. 26-cv-1099 (Oct. 2, 2026)

(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
No. _______
MARKWAYNE MULLIN, ET AL., APPLICANTS
v.
FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH, ET AL.
───────────
APPLICATION FOR A STAY OF THE INJUNCTION
ISSUED BY THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE WESTERN DISTRICT OF TEXAS
───────────
Pursuant to Rule 23 of the Rules of this Court and the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C.
1651, the Solicitor General, on behalf of Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland
Security, et al., respectfully requests that this Court stay the preliminary injunction
issued by the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas (App.,
infra, 202a-203a), pending the timely filing and disposition of a petition for a writ of
certiorari in this Court.1  In addition to a stay, the Solicitor General also respectfully
requests that this Court treat this application as a petition for a writ of certiorari,
grant the petition, and summarily reverse.
This case involves a baseless injunction that halts a major portion of the con-
struction of the border wall.  Decades ago, Congress enacted legislation to make it
easier for the Executive Branch to engage in such construction to protect against il-
1  An appeal to the court of appeals is not available.  Under Section 102(c)(2)(C) of
the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, as added
by the REAL ID Act of 2005, Pub. L. No. 109-13, § 102, 119 Stat. 306, the district
court’s injunction “may be reviewed only upon petition for a writ of certiorari to the
Supreme Court of the United States.”  See pp. 8, 24, infra.

2
legal entry, and to make it harder for federal judges to block those critical national-
security endeavors.  Congress specifically granted the Attorney General (and now,
the Secretary of Homeland Security) broad authority in the Immigration Reform and
Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) to construct border barriers and roads
“to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry,” and expressly authorized the
Secretary “to waive all legal requirements” that he “determines necessary to ensure
expeditious construction of the barriers and roads under this section.”  Pub. L. No.
104-208, Div. C, Tit. I, § 102(a), 110 Stat. 3009-554; IIRIRA § 102(c)(1), as amended
by the REAL ID Act of 2005, Pub. L. No. 109-13, Div. B, Tit. I, § 102, 119 Stat. 306
(8 U.S.C. 1103 note).2  To further guard against delays in border-wall construction,
Congress stripped federal courts of jurisdiction to hear any non-constitutional chal-
lenges to a Secretary’s waiver decision.  IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(C).
Pursuant to this authority, the Secretary issued three waivers in 2026 to facil-
itate expeditious border barrier and road construction in Texas, in the region that
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has designated the Big Bend Sector.  App.,
infra, 2a, 4a, 7a.  The Big Bend Sector covers nearly one quarter of the U.S.-Mexico
border; these waivers facilitated urgently needed construction of border walls and
roads spanning over 300 miles.  The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector “is an
area of high illegal entry” requiring additional border barriers, and thus waived the
application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws in order to facilitate
expeditious border-wall construction in that Sector.  Ibid.  The record amply bears
out those concerns:  between fiscal years 2021 and 2025, CBP apprehended over
2  As discussed below (at 8), Congress amended Section 102(c) of IIRIRA in the
REAL ID Act.  Unless otherwise indicated, all citations of IIRIRA Section 102(c) or
its subprovisions in this application refer to the statute as amended or added by
REAL ID Act § 102, 119 Stat. 306 (8 U.S.C. 1103 note).

3
89,000 aliens attempting to enter here—and those are just the aliens who were de-
tected.  App., infra, 226a-227a.  CBP seized enormous amounts of fentanyl, heroin,
methamphetamine, cocaine, and marijuana—and seizures have only grown in fiscal
year 2026.  Id. at 18a, 226a-227a.  The Sinaloa and Juarez cartels operate south of
this sector across the Mexico border and seek to exploit any vulnerabilities in United
States border protection to traffic humans, drugs, and weapons across the border and
infiltrate the United States.  See id. at 227a.  Moreover, leaving a 300-plus-mile gap
in border defenses would act as a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors
to exploit as other routes close off.  See id. at 226a.
On October 2, 2026, the district court nonetheless issued an unprecedented
injunction blocking those waivers and halting associated border-wall construction.
The court enjoined the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from engaging in
any border-wall construction in the Big Bend Sector unless and until the government
complies with environmental and other laws.  The injunction deemed unlawful and
stayed the effectiveness of the Secretary’s waiver decisions that had enabled that
construction.  Yet, for nearly two weeks, the district court declined to offer any expla-
nation for that sweeping injunction beyond the unreasoned assertion that respond-
ents were “likely to succeed on the merits of at least one” of their claims, without
specifying which one.  App., infra, 202a; but see Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(d)(1)(A) (“Every
order granting an injunction  * * *  must  * * *  state the reasons why it issued.”).
The court’s written opinion, issued October 14, finally divulged some reasoning
for its far-reaching shutdown of border-wall construction, see App., infra, 204a-217a—
but that reasoning is untenable.  On the merits, the sole basis for this injunction was
the district court’s belief that the Secretary lacked “clear congressional authoriza-
tion,” supposedly required by the major-questions doctrine, to issue the waivers.

4
App., infra, 211a.  In the court’s view, the waivers exceeded the Secretary’s authority
under IIRIRA to construct barriers and issue waivers for areas of “high illegal entry,”
because the number of illegal-alien apprehensions in Big Bend is comparatively lower
than in other sectors of the border.  Id. at 214a.
That is exactly the kind of claim that Congress denied district courts jurisdic-
tion to entertain.  IIRIRA allows only claims “alleging a violation of the Constitution.”
§ 102(c)(2)(A).  But the major-questions doctrine is used to determine “whether Con-
gress in fact meant to confer the power the agency has asserted,” West Virginia v.
EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 721 (2022), or whether the agency instead exceeded its statutory
authority.  As this Court has long held, claims that an agency exceeded its statutory
authority are not constitutional claims.  See Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462, 472
(1994).
Beyond that fatal jurisdictional defect, this major-questions claim borders on
frivolous.  Congress was hardly shy about the major powers it granted the Secretary.
IIRIRA addresses head-on whether the Secretary can waive legal requirements such
as those found in Endangered Species Act of 1973, 16 U.S.C. 1531 et seq., and the
National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq., by ex-
pressly authorizing the Secretary to issue waivers like the Big Bend waivers.  Nor
are the waivers here unusual:  the Secretary has issued waivers like these repeatedly
for decades.  Even the district court acknowledged that Congress granted the Secre-
tary some waiver power, see App., infra, 212a; the court just effectively rewrote
IIRIRA to atextually limit the Secretary’s waiver authority to only areas of “compar-
ative[ly]” high illegal entry, id. at 214a (emphasis added).
Compounding its errors, the district court severely misbalanced the equities.
In denying a stay pending certiorari, the district court begrudgingly acknowledged

5
that the government “will experience at least some degree of irreparable harm absent
a stay” because the injunction will “continue to prevent[ ]” the government “from ef-
fectuating [its] policies.”  App., infra, 236a.  Left unstated, however, is what those
harms entail:  disruption of the government’s ability to secure a quarter of the south-
ern border against cartel incursions, drug trafficking, and illegal entry; creation of a
massive vulnerability in border protection that risks funneling illegal entry and traf-
ficking into the unsecured Big Bend Sector; and irreversible delays, costs, and oper-
ational harms from halting already-begun construction.
By eliding the government’s harms, the court illogically concluded that re-
spondents’ aesthetic and recreational harms “outweigh” the government’s extraordi-
narily strong border-security and operational interests in ensuring that 25% of the
U.S.-Mexico border has adequate protective barriers.  The notion that respondents’
interest in “ ‘escap[ing] from modern life’ ” in the “wild spaces in the Big Bend Sector”
and preserving “the spiritual, recreational, and aesthetic value of the area,” App.,
infra, 216a, surpasses the United States’ paramount interest in preventing a quarter
of the border from becoming a magnet for cartel exploitation defies credulity.  Indeed,
this Court has already rejected a similar misbalancing of the equities when it previ-
ously granted a stay of a preliminary injunction that prevented border-wall construc-
tion.  Trump v. Sierra Club, 588 U.S. 930 (2019).  Though that injunction did not
involve Secretarial waivers, the same equities were in play:  the government objected
to the devastating national-security effects of preventing it from constructing a bor-
der wall, while the Sierra Club plaintiffs asserted countervailing aesthetic and recre-
ational interests. In granting that stay, the Court necessarily concluded that the eq-
uities balanced in the government’s favor.  So too here, the government’s sovereign

6
interests in protecting the border and effectuating Congress’s mandate to engage in
border-wall construction to deter illegal entry vastly outweighs respondents’ harms.
The end result is a district-court injunction that is both unlawful and unprec-
edented.  Until now, no court has ever sustained a challenge to the substance of a
Secretary’s Section 102(c) waiver decision.  Many judges have rejected such chal-
lenges.  See Center for Biological Diversity v. McAleenan, 404 F. Supp. 3d 218 (D.D.C.
2019) (K.B. Jackson, J.), cert. denied, 591 U.S. 1015 (2020).  Only this district court
has seen fit to trample Congress’s clear authorization of waivers to facilitate border-
wall construction and its equally clear judicial-review bar by repackaging a statutory-
authority argument in constitutional garb.  Such judicial usurpation of Congress’s
commands and the Secretary’s authority amply warrants a stay.  Given the manifest
errors in the district court’s decision, this Court should also grant certiorari and sum-
marily reverse the order of the district court granting a preliminary injunction.
STATEMENT
A.
Legal Background
DHS is responsible for securing our Nation’s borders and detecting and pre-
venting illegal entry into the United States.  See 6 U.S.C. 202(1) and (2).  In the
Secure Fence Act of 2006 (Secure Fence Act), Pub. L. No. 109-367, 120 Stat. 2638,
Congress expressly directed DHS to “take all actions the Secretary determines nec-
essary and appropriate to achieve and maintain operational control over the entire
international land  * * *  border[ ] of the United States.”  § 2(a) (8 U.S.C. 1701 note).
The statute defines “ ‘operational control’ ” to mean “the prevention of all unlawful
entries into the United States, including entries by terrorists, other unlawful aliens,
instruments of terrorism, narcotics, and other contraband.”  § 2(b).

7
1.  Among other means of carrying out that mission, Congress granted DHS
broad authority to construct border barriers and roads under Section 102 of IIRIRA.
That provision works as follows:
Section 102(a) directs the Secretary to “take such actions as may be necessary
to install additional physical barriers and roads (including the removal of obstacles
to detection of illegal entrants) in the vicinity of the United States border to deter
illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.”  IIRIRA
§ 102(a), 110 Stat. 3009-554 (8 U.S.C. 1103 note).3
Section 102(b) directs DHS to construct barriers in specific geographic areas
that Congress deemed to be a priority.  As originally enacted in 1996, Section 102(b)
required the construction of certain “fences” and “roads” in a 14-mile section of the
border near San Diego.  110 Stat. 3009-554.  Later amendments focused on other
areas of illegal entry.  In 2006, for example, Congress struck the reference to San
Diego and instead required construction of at “least 2 layers of reinforced fencing”
and other construction in five locations along the southern border.  Secure Fence Act
§ 3(2)(A), 120 Stat. 2639.  Most recently, in December 2007, Congress replaced its
2006 directive with a broader, currently operative mandate to construct “reinforced
fencing along not less than 700 miles of the southwest border.”  Consolidated Appro-
priations Act of 2008, Pub. L. No. 110-161, Div. E, Tit. V, § 564(a)(2)(B)(ii), 121 Stat.
2090.  The Secretary retains the discretion to determine that the use or placement of
“fencing, physical barriers, roads, lighting, cameras, and sensors in a particular loca-
3  IIRIRA initially tasked the Attorney General with implementing Section 102.
See 110 Stat. 3009-554.  When Congress created DHS, it transferred the Attorney
General’s powers and duties to “control and guard the boundaries and borders of the
United States against the illegal entry of aliens” to the Secretary.  8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1)
and (5); see 6 U.S.C. 251, 291.

8
tion” is not “the most appropriate means to achieve and maintain operational control
over the international border” at that location.  121 Stat. 2091.
Section 102(c) expressly vests the Secretary with the waiver authority at is-
sue here.  Recognizing that compliance with certain laws can slow the pace of federal
construction projections, Section 102(c) grants the Secretary “the authority to waive
all legal requirements such Secretary, in such Secretary’s sole discretion, determines
necessary to ensure expeditious construction of the barriers and roads under this sec-
tion.”  IIRIRA § 102(c)(1).  As originally enacted in 1996, Section 102(c) authorized
the waiver of two statutes’ legal requirements:  “the Endangered Species Act of 1973
and the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.”  110 Stat. 3009-555.  In the
REAL ID Act of 2005, Congress expanded the Secretary’s waiver authority to include
“all legal requirements.”  § 102, 119 Stat. 306; see H.R. Rep. No. 72, 109th Cong., 1st
Sess. 171 (2005) (Conf. Rep.) (explaining intent to extend the Secretary’s waiver au-
thority “to any local, state or federal statute, regulation, or administrative order that
could impede expeditious construction of border security infrastructure”).
Section 102(c) also expressly limits judicial review of such waivers.  Congress
provided that the federal district courts have “exclusive jurisdiction” over a claim
arising from the Secretary’s exercise of the waiver authority, but a “claim may only
be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States.”  IIRIRA
§ 102(c)(2)(A).  Congress added that “[t]he court shall not have jurisdiction to hear
any claim not specified in this subparagraph,”—that is, any claim that does not allege
a constitutional violation.  Ibid.  Congress further provided that any claim authorized
under Section 102(c)(2)(A) must be brought within 60 days after the Secretary’s
waiver decision, and that any district court decision is reviewable only through a writ
of certiorari from this Court.  IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(B) and (C); see p. 1 n.1, supra.

9
2.  Since the transfer of waiver authority from the Attorney General to DHS in
2005, the Secretary has repeatedly issued waiver determinations under IIRIRA Sec-
tion 102(c) to ensure the expeditious construction of barriers and roads along the
southern border.  See, e.g., 90 Fed. Reg. 23,946 (June 5, 2025); 84 Fed. Reg. 21,798
(May 15, 2019); 82 Fed. Reg. 35,984 (Aug. 2, 2017); 73 Fed. Reg. 19,078 (Apr. 8, 2008);
72 Fed. Reg. 60,870 (Oct. 26, 2007); 70 Fed. Reg. 55,622 (Sept. 22, 2005).  CBP informs
this Office that there have been over 60 such waiver determinations since 2005.  To
date, every attempted constitutional challenge to the Secretary’s Section 102(c) au-
thority to issue waiver determinations has failed.4
B.
The Big Bend Waivers
In 2026, the Secretary issued three waivers to expedite barrier construction
along the southern border in Texas, in CBP’s Big Bend Sector.  The Big Bend Sector
spans 165,154 square miles and includes 517 miles of riverfront on the Rio Grande
separating the United States from Mexico—almost one quarter of the southwest bor-
der.

and
Border
Protection,
Big
Bend
Sector
Texas,
https://perma.cc/CCX2-ZXY2.
Then-Secretary Noem issued the first of these “Big Bend waivers” on February
17, 2026, for a project area in which CBP is planning to construct about 164 miles of
border barrier system.  91 Fed. Reg. 7297 (Feb. 17, 2026), as amended by 91 Fed. Reg.
4  See, e.g., Center for Biological Diversity v. Mullin, No. cv-25-365, 2026 WL
836278 (D. Ariz. Mar. 26, 2026); Center for Biological Diversity v. McAleenan, 404 F.
Supp. 3d 218 (D.D.C. 2019) (K.B. Jackson, J.), cert. denied, 591 U.S. 1015 (2020); In

sub nom. Animal Legal Def. Fund v. Department of Homeland Sec., 586 U.S. 1035
(2018); County of El Paso v. Chertoff, No. 08-CA-196, 2008 WL 11417030 (W.D. Tex.
Sept. 11, 2008), cert. denied, 557 U.S. 915 (2009); Save Our Heritage Org. v. Gonzalez,
533 F. Supp. 2d 58 (D.D.C. 2008); Defenders of Wildlife v. Chertoff, 527 F. Supp. 2d
119 (D.D.C. 2007), cert. denied, 554 U.S. 918 (2008); Sierra Club v. Ashcroft, No. 04-
CV-272, 2005 WL 8153059 (S.D. Cal. Dec. 13, 2005).

10
40,550 (July 2, 2026) (App., infra, 4a-5a); see D. Ct. Doc. 38-1, ¶¶ 18-20 (Aug. 24,
2026) (First Enriquez Decl.).  On May 15, 2026, Secretary Mullin issued a second
waiver for another project area in which CBP is planning to construct roads and about
17 miles of non-contiguous vehicle barrier system in Big Bend National Park.  91 Fed.
Reg. 27,969 (May 15, 2026), as amended by 91 Fed. Reg. 34,831 (June 9, 2026) (App.,
infra, 1a-3a); see First Enriquez Decl. ¶ 9.  On July 27, 2026, Secretary Mullin issued
a third waiver for a project area in which CBP is planning to construct about 160
miles of barrier system in the Big Bend Sector and the nearby Del Rio Sector.  91 Fed.
Reg. 46,939 (July 27, 2026) (App., infra, 6a-8a); see First Enriquez Decl. ¶ 22; see also
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Del Rio Sector Texas, https://perma.cc/NAM6-
8SR4.
In each of these waiver decisions, the Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector
“is an area of high illegal entry,” and that constructing additional barriers and roads
is necessary to fulfill DHS’s statutory mandate to achieve operational control of the
border.  App., infra, 2a, 4a, 7a.  The waiver decisions explained that between 2021
and 2025, the U.S. Border Patrol “apprehended over 89,000 illegal aliens attempting
to enter the United States between border crossings in the Big Bend Sector,” and
during that same period “seized over 87,574 pounds of marijuana, over 867 pounds of
cocaine, over 1,156 pounds of methamphetamine, over 12 pounds of heroin, and over
94 pounds of fentanyl.”  Ibid.  The Secretary found that each specified project area
within the Big Bend Sector is itself “an area of high illegal entry.”  Ibid.  The Secretary
thus waived the applicability of “all federal, state, or other laws, regulations and legal
requirements of, deriving from, or related to the subject of ” specified federal statutes
in the covered project areas.  Ibid.

11
C.
Proceedings Below
In April 2026, respondents—an individual Big Bend river guide, an environ-
mental nonprofit, and a nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving a historic
church in Ruidosa, Texas—filed a complaint challenging the lawfulness of the Big
Bend waiver decisions.  See D. Ct. Doc. 1 (Apr. 16, 2026).  Respondents’ complaint, as
subsequently amended and supplemented, alleges that the waivers violate the major
questions doctrine, the nondelegation doctrine, the Take Care Clause, the Fifth
Amendment’s Due Process Clause, and the Presentment Clause.  See D. Ct. Doc. 26,
¶¶ 76-113 (Aug. 11, 2026) (Am. Supp. Compl.).  The parties and the court agreed to
resolve the case on cross-motions for summary judgment.  See D. Ct. Doc. 16 (June
23, 2026).  In August 2026, while those motions were pending, respondents moved for
a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order that would enjoin the gov-
ernment from constructing border barriers in Big Bend Sector pursuant to the chal-
lenged waivers.  D. Ct. Doc. 34 (Aug. 17, 2026) (P.I. Mot.).
On October 2, 2026, the district court held a hearing on respondents’ motion,
during which witnesses for respondents presented testimony.  See App., infra, 26a-
201a.  The court then issued a preliminary injunction enjoining applicants from
“build[ing] border barrier or related infrastructure, or engag[ing] in any construction
or ground disturbing activities, in the Big Bend Sector until and unless [applicants]
comply with all applicable laws,” “notwithstanding the ‘Big Bend Waivers.’ ”  Id. at
202a.  The order further stated that respondents are “likely to succeed on the merits
of at least one of the claims in suit,” but it did not identify which claim supported the
injunction.  Ibid.  The order instead promised that a “memorandum opinion will fol-
low” explaining the court’s “rationale in greater detail.”  Ibid.

12
CBP immediately notified contractors for the Big Bend construction projects to
suspend all construction and ground-disturbing activities in the Big Bend Sector,
App., infra, 219a, despite the lack of any memorandum opinion explaining the basis
for the injunction.  When the district court still had not issued an opinion six days
later, the government filed a motion requesting that the court issue an opinion and
stay its injunction pending review in this Court.  See D. Ct. Doc. 74 (Oct. 8, 2026).
The government’s motion explained that the court’s unreasoned order violated the
Federal Rules of Civil Procedure—specifically Rule 52(a)(2), which requires a court
“granting or refusing an interlocutory injunction” to “state the findings and conclu-
sions that support its action,” Fed. R. Civ. P. 52(a)(2); and Rule 65(d), which provides
that “[e]very order granting an injunction” must “state the reasons why it issued,”
Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(d)(1)(A).  See D. Ct. Doc. 74, at 2-3.  The motion further explained
that a stay was warranted under the traditional factors for a stay pending a writ of
certiorari—including because all of respondents’ theories for rejecting the waivers
lacked merit, and the injunction causes the government irreparable harm.  Id. at 3-16.
On October 14, 2026, the district court finally issued a memorandum opinion
supplying the reasons for the injunction it had ordered 12 days earlier.  App., infra,
204a-217a.  The opinion stated that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits
of their claim that the Big Bend waivers violated the major-questions doctrine.  Id. at
214a.  The government had argued that the court lacked jurisdiction over the major-
questions claim because it does not “alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the
United States,” IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A).  See App., infra, 207a.  The court disagreed,
holding that “the major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear statement rule
grounded in separation of powers,” such that respondent’s major-questions-doctrine
claim “alleges a Constitutional violation.”  Id. at 210a-211a.

13
The district court then determined that the waivers violated the major-ques-
tions doctrine because the Secretary lacked “ ‘clear congressional authorization’ to is-
sue the Big Bend” waivers.  App., infra, 211a.  The court interpreted the Secretary’s
waiver authority to reach “only construction ‘to deter illegal crossings in areas of high
illegal entry.’ ”  Id. at 212a.  The court determined that the Big Bend waivers did not
qualify on the theory that migrant apprehensions are comparatively lower in the Big
Bend Sector than in other sectors along the U.S.-Mexico border.  Id. at 214a.
The district court further determined that plaintiffs suffered a substantial
threat of irreparable harm without a preliminary injunction.  App., infra, 215a-216a.
The court found that border-barrier construction pursuant to the waivers would “re-
strict” the “livelihoods” of certain respondents, specifically mentioning two river
guides and a rancher.  Id. at 215a.  The court also found that construction of a border
barrier would cause “harm to the natural ecosystem, including local wildlife,” id. at
216a, citing, inter alia, “a dramatic uptick in roadkill” attributed to contractors’ vehi-
cles.  Ibid.  And the court credited testimony that border-barrier construction in Big
Bend would “deteriorate the spiritual, recreational, and aesthetic value of the area.”
Ibid.  On the other hand, the court asserted that the government would “only suffer
a temporary delay while this Court assesses the merits of the pending summary judg-
ment motions.”  Id. at 217a.  The court did not acknowledge the harm of shutting
down about 340 miles of planned barrier and road construction indefinitely.
On October 21, 2026, the district court denied applicants’ motion to stay the
injunction pending disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari in this Court.  App.,
infra, 233a-238a.  The district court acknowledged that “because they will continue
to be prevented from effectuating their policies,” the government defendants “have
demonstrated that they will experience at least some degree of irreparable harm ab-

14
sent a stay.”  Id. at 236a.  But the court concluded that the other factors under Nken
v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 426 (2009), counseled against a stay.  App., infra, 236a.  The
court determined that the government’s “likelihood of success on appeal is low.”  Id.
at 235a.  And the court found that the government’s injuries were outweighed by the
“irreversible environmental, aesthetic, economic, and recreational harms” that re-
spondents would supposedly suffer without an injunction.  Id. at 236a.
ARGUMENT
Under Rule 23 of the Rules of this Court and the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. 1651,
to obtain a stay of an injunction pending appellate proceedings, an applicant must
show a likelihood of success on the merits, a reasonable probability of obtaining cer-
tiorari, and a likelihood of irreparable harm.  See Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S.
183, 190 (2010) (per curiam).  All of those factors strongly favor a stay here.
I.
THE GOVERNMENT IS HIGHLY LIKELY TO SUCCEED ON THE MERITS
 The district court enjoined the government’s border-wall construction in the
Big Bend Sector on the ground that the Secretary lacked the “clear congressional
authorization” required under the major-questions doctrine to issue the Big Bend
waivers.  App., infra, 211a.  That order is comprehensively flawed.  First, the court
lacked jurisdiction over this claim.  IIRIRA limits federal jurisdiction in challenges to
Section 102(c) waivers to claims “alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United
States,” IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(C), but the major-questions doctrine is a tool for evaluat-
ing alleged statutory violations.  Further, respondents’ major-questions claim is
plainly wrong on the merits.  The Secretary’s waiver authority reflects a crystal-clear,
indisputably valid express delegation from Congress that the Executive has used for
decades to expedite border-wall construction.

15
A.
The District Court Lacked Jurisdiction Over Respondents’ Major-
Questions Claim
1.
Congress granted the Secretary broad authority to “waive all legal re-
quirements” that he deems necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border
barriers and roads, IIRIRA § 102(c)(1), and then strictly limited federal-court juris-
diction over challenges to such waiver decisions.  Specifically, a “cause of action or
claim” arising from a Secretary’s waiver decision “may only be brought alleging a
violation of the Constitution of the United States.”  IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A).  Further, a
“court shall not have jurisdiction to hear any claim not specified in this subpara-
graph.”  § 102(c)(2)(C).  Taken together, those provisions deprive federal courts of ju-
risdiction over all challenges to IIRIRA waiver decisions except those “alleging a vio-
lation of the Constitution.”  See Center for Biological Diversity v. McAleenan, 404 F.
Supp. 3d 218, 235, 237 (D.D.C. 2019) (K.B. Jackson, J.) (“Congress has  * * *  expressly
deprived the federal courts of jurisdiction over non-constitutional claims that chal-
lenge DHS’s section 102(c) waiver decisions.”), cert. denied, 591 U.S. 1015 (2020).
That express jurisdictional bar on non-constitutional claims should have
doomed respondents’ major-questions claim, and the district court seriously erred in
holding otherwise.  App., infra, 214a.  The major-questions doctrine helps determine
whether Congress “meant to confer” on the Executive Branch “the authority it claims”
under a particular statute.  West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 725 (2022).  Though
animated in part by “separation of powers principles,” id. at 723, the doctrine oper-
ates to resolve whether the Executive Branch has exceeded its statutory authority.
This Court’s recent major-questions cases illustrate how the doctrine works:

16
 West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 735, applied the major-questions doctrine to de-
termine that an emissions-reduction system adopted by EPA fell outside
“the authority granted to the Agency in Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act.”
 Alabama Ass’n of Realtors v. HHS, 594 U.S. 758, 764 (2021) (per curiam),
applied the doctrine to reject the government’s argument that “§ 361(a) [of
the Public Health Services Act] gives the CDC the authority to impose [an]
eviction moratorium.”
 NFIB v. OSHA, 595 U.S. 109, 117 (2022) (per curiam), applied the doctrine
to conclude that the “authority that Congress has provided” to the Secretary
of Labor in the Occupational Safety and Health Act, 29 U.S.C. 651 et seq.,
likely did not include the power to mandate that certain workers be vac-
cinated or regularly tested for COVID-19.
 Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477, 506 (2023), applied the doctrine to confirm
that the “HEROES Act provides no authorization for the” Secretary of Ed-
ucation’s student-loan cancellation plan.
 Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, 255 (2026), applied the
doctrine to determine that “IEEPA [International Emergency Economic
Powers Act] does not authorize the President to impose tariffs.”
In each case, the major-questions doctrine guided the Court’s inquiry into whether
the government had exceeded its authority under a statute, not the Constitution.
Here too, respondents invoke the major-questions doctrine in service of alleg-
ing a statutory—not constitutional—violation.  The count of their operative complaint
alleging a “violation of the major questions doctrine” claims that the Secretary’s use
of waivers to build a border wall exceeds his authority under IIRIRA.  See Am. Supp.
Compl. ¶ 85 (contending that border-wall construction “exceeds Congress’s grant of

17
authority”); see id. ¶ 81 (“[T]he text of IIRIRA contains no clear grant of authority for
such a significant project.”).  The district court’s opinion confirms the statutory nature
of respondents’ claim.  See App., infra, 211a.  The court found that respondents were
likely to succeed on their major-questions-doctrine claim on the theory that the Sec-
retary lacked “clear congressional authorization” to issue the Big Bend waivers.  Ibid.
(emphasis added); see id. at 214a.  The court concluded that the Secretary exceeded
his powers under IIRIRA by authorizing waivers in a sector that the court determined
not to be an area of “high illegal entry” within the meaning of the statute.  Id. at 214a.
As this Court has long held, a claim that alleges that an Executive Branch
official acted “in excess of his statutory authority” is not a claim alleging a “violation
of the Constitution.”  Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462, 472 (1994).  Dalton thus rejected
the court of appeals’ theory that “whenever the President acts in excess of his statu-
tory authority, he also violates the constitutional separation-of-powers doctrine.”  Id.
at 469, 471.  The Court explained that “claims simply alleging that the President has
exceeded his statutory authority are not ‘constitutional’ claims, subject to judicial re-
view under the exception recognized in” Franklin v. Massachusetts, 505 U.S. 788
(1992).  Dalton, 511 U.S. at 473-474.  Otherwise, “if every claim alleging that the
President exceeded his statutory authority were considered a constitutional claim,
the exception” permitting review of only constitutional claims “would be broadened
beyond recognition.”  Id. at 474.
The same principle applies here:  Claims that the Secretary has exceeded his
waiver authority under IIRIRA—whether grounded in the major-questions doctrine
or any other principle of statutory interpretation—are not claims “alleging a violation
of the Constitution of the United States,” IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A).  Treating them that
way would “eviscerat[e]” the limitations on federal jurisdiction of waiver decisions

18
that Congress carefully drew in Section 102(c).  Dalton, 511 U.S. at 474.  The district
court thus did “not have jurisdiction” to hear such a claim.  IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(C).
2.
The district court resisted that straightforward analysis.  Instead, the
court reasoned that because the major-questions doctrine has constitutional under-
pinnings, respondents had alleged a constitutional claim.  App., infra, 209a-211a.
That conclusion does not follow.  Many canons and rules of statutory interpretation
reflect constitutional principles, from the federalism canon to the clear-statement
rule for abrogations of sovereign immunity.  See Learning Resources, 607 U.S. at 279
(Gorsuch, J., concurring).  But relying on those commonplace rules of statutory inter-
pretation does not mean a court has adjudicated a constitutional claim.  Indeed, that
is the whole point of the canon of constitutional avoidance, which also shares consti-
tutional underpinnings but has as a key purpose “to avoid the decision of constitu-
tional questions.”  Clark v. Martinez, 543 U.S. 371, 381-382 (2005).  Respondents have
similarly characterized the major-questions doctrine as an avoidance doctrine that
“protect[s] the Constitution” by avoiding an interpretation that, if adopted, “ ‘would
deal a severe blow to the Constitution’s separation of powers.’ ”  D. Ct. Doc. 77, at 15
(Oct. 20, 2026) (Stay Opp.) (quoting Utility Air, 573 U.S. at 327).  But invoking con-
stitutional avoidance is “not a method of adjudicating constitutional questions by
other means”; instead, when a litigant invokes that canon “he seeks to vindicate his
own statutory rights.”  Clark, 543 U.S. at 381.  The same is true when a litigant in-
vokes the major-questions doctrine.
The district court’s digressions into whether the major-questions doctrine is “ ‘a
substantive clear-statement rule’ or ‘a purely linguistic canon of construction,’ ” are
thus irrelevant to whether a major-questions-based objection to the waivers is a con-
stitutional claim.  App., infra, 210a (citation omitted).  Under no theory does respond-

19
ents’ major-questions claim “alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United
States.”  IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(C).  Even separate writings by Members of the Court that
the district court cited as adopting a “constitutional clear statement rule” theory of
the major-questions doctrine still treat the doctrine as a tool for evaluating an alleged
statutory violation.  App., infra, 210a.  For example, Justice Gorsuch’s concurrence
in Learning Resources explained that the “central question in any major questions
case” is whether the Executive Branch’s claimed power is “supported by clear statu-
tory authority.”  607 U.S. at 283 (emphasis added).
This Court thus need not resolve “heady question[s]” about the theoretical un-
derpinnings of the major-questions doctrine, App., infra, 208a (citation omitted), to
reject the district court’s analysis.  Under any theory, the government is likely to
succeed on the merits because respondents’ major-questions claim alleges a statutory
violation, not a constitutional claim.  See Dalton, 511 U.S. at 474.  The district court
accordingly lacked jurisdiction to grant relief to respondents on that claim.
B.
The Major-Questions Doctrine Does Not Preclude These Waivers
1.
Even setting that dispositive jurisdictional defect aside, respondents’
major-questions claim is meritless.  The major-questions doctrine prescribes that in
“extraordinary cases” involving assertions of “vast economic and political signifi-
cance” or “ ‘extravagant statutory power over the national economy,’ ” courts must look
for a “ ‘clear’ ” indication that Congress actually intended to delegate the broad statu-
tory authority asserted.  West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 716, 723-724 (citations omitted).
An agency’s assertion of an “unheralded” or newfound power “representing a ‘trans-
formative expansion’ ” in its “ ‘regulatory authority’ ” thus warrants skepticism.  Id. at
724 (quoting Utility Air Regulatory Grp. v. EPA, 573 U.S. 302, 324 (2014)).

20
This is no major-questions case.  Even assuming that the Secretary’s waiver
authority implicates a question of “vast economic and political significance,” Congress
did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal
requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.  IIRIRA Section
102(a) instructs DHS to “take such actions as may be necessary to install additional
physical barriers and roads  * * *  in the vicinity of the United States border to deter
illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.”  IIRIRA
§ 102(a), 110 Stat. 3009-554.  Section 102(b) further directs the agency to “construct
reinforced fencing along not less than 700 miles of the southwest border.”  IIRIRA
§ 102(b), as amended by Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2008 § 564(a)(2)(B)(ii),
121 Stat. 2090.  And Section 102(c) expressly authorizes the Secretary to “waive all
legal requirements [the] Secretary, in such Secretary’s sole discretion, determines
necessary to ensure expeditious construction of the barriers and roads under this sec-
tion.”  IIRIRA § 102(c)(1) (emphasis added).  Congress’s delegations of authority could
not be more express.
Nor is DHS’s reliance on its waiver authority to construct border barriers some
“ ‘newfound’ ” power “outside its wheelhouse.”  Biden, 600 U.S. at 518-519 (Barrett, J.,
concurring).  The Secretary has repeatedly exercised his waiver authority to construct
border barriers for over 20 years.  See pp. 8-9, supra.  And that authority falls
squarely within DHS’s border-security mission.  That long history of agency action,
pursuant to an express statutory delegation, does not remotely resemble cases that
have triggered the major-questions doctrine, such as the CDC’s imposition of an evic-
tion moratorium or OSHA’s imposition of a vaccine mandate.  See Alabama Ass’n of
Realtors, 594 U.S. at 764; NFIB, 595 U.S. at 113.

21
2.
Tellingly, given Congress’s express delegation, neither the district court
nor respondents have suggested that the major-questions doctrine precludes the Sec-
retary from constructing border barriers or issuing waiver decisions altogether.  In-
stead, respondents’ major-questions claim challenges only these specific Big Bend
waivers on the theory that the Big Bend Sector is not an “area[ ] of high illegal entry”
as the statute requires.  IIRIRA § 102(a), 110 Stat. 3009-554; see P.I. Mot. 10.  That
is not even a major-questions argument; it is a minor question about the scope of
statutory provisions that unquestionably authorize waivers writ large.  Respondents
insist that the Big Bend waivers supposedly differ from prior waivers in “magnitude,”
if not in kind.  Stay Opp. 18 (quoting Biden, 600 U.S. at 501).  But respondents do not
actually contend that any Big Bend waiver is meaningfully greater in scope than prior
waiver decisions, only that DHS has not previously found the entire Big Bend Sector
to be an area of “high illegal entry.”  Id. at 17.  That just underscores that respondents’
claim rests on an anodyne interpretive question about how a broad delegation of au-
thority applies to a particular case, not whether the agency possesses a major power
at all.
Regardless, this argument fails on its own terms.  IIRIRA assigns to the Sec-
retary the authority to determine whether it is “necessary to install additional phys-
ical barriers and roads” near the border “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high
illegal entry into the United States.”  IIRIRA § 102(a), 110 Stat. 3009-554.  That au-
thority necessarily implies the corresponding authority to determine which border
segments are “areas of high illegal entry.”  In each of the three waiver decisions at
issue, the Secretary appropriately exercised that discretion by finding that Big Bend
Sector as a whole and each specified project area within Big Bend Sector were areas
of “high illegal entry.”  App., infra, 2a, 4a, 7a.  That determination was supported by

22
the Secretary’s findings that massive quantities of drugs were seized in Big Bend
Sector between fiscal year 2021 and fiscal year 2025, and that 89,000 illegal aliens
were apprehended in the region during that period.  Ibid.
The district court nevertheless held that the Secretary’s waiver decisions vio-
lated IIRIRA.  The court did not dispute that there had been a high volume of appre-
hensions and “similarly large quantities of drugs seized” in the Big Bend Sector.
App., infra, 214a.  But in the court’s view, that was not enough to make the Big Bend
Sector an area of “high illegal entry” under the statute, because illegal-alien crossings
and drug trafficking are comparatively less common in the Big Bend Sector than in
other sectors along the U.S.-Mexico border.  Id. at 213a-214a.
That conclusion amounts to a judicial rewrite of Congress’s words in Section
102.  Instead of authorizing the Secretary to construct barriers and issue waivers in
all “areas of high illegal entry,” the court read the statute to cover only areas of com-
paratively high illegal entry, as measured against nearby areas on the same border.
But courts “may not narrow a provision’s reach by inserting words Congress chose to
omit.”  Lomax v. Ortiz-Marquez, 140 S. Ct. 1721, 1725 (2020).  Nothing in the lan-
guage that Congress actually wrote precludes the Secretary from determining that a
segment of the U.S.-Mexico border is an “area[ ] of high illegal entry,” even if other
nearby segments have even higher illegal entry.  See In re Border Infrastructure En-
vtl. Litig., 915 F.3d 1213, 1224 (9th Cir. 2019) (“IIRIRA does not dictate that ‘high
illegal entry’ is a comparative determination.”).  Even the lowest rates of entry along
the southern border are extraordinarily “high” in both an absolute and an historical
sense, given the massive scale of illegal entries in recent years.  See generally Proc-
lamation 10,886, Declaring a National Emergency at the Southern Border of the
United States, 90 Fed. Reg. 8327 (Jan. 29, 2025).

23
The district court rejected that interpretation on the grounds that the statu-
tory word “ ‘high’ ” itself implies a “comparative dimension.”  App., infra, 214a.  The
court further believed that the statutory limitation to “areas of high illegal entry”
would be meaningless if the Secretary could designate the entire U.S.-Mexico border
such an area.  Ibid.  But IIRIRA empowers the Secretary to build barriers and issue
waivers for any region that he finds to have high illegal entry without remotely sug-
gesting that the Secretary must undertake any kind of comparative assessment.
Quite the contrary, Congress made clear that Section 102 is a tool for the Secretary
to
gain
“operational
control”
over
the
Nation’s
borders,
IIRIRA
§ 102(b)(1)(A) and (D), as amended by Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2008
§ 564(a)(2)(B)(ii), 121 Stat. 2090-2091—a term that means “the prevention of all un-
lawful entries,” Secure Fence Act of 2006 § 2(b), 120 Stat. 2638 (emphasis added).
The district court’s statutory overhaul would also produce wildly implausible
consequences.  In the court’s view, Congress permitted the Secretary to build border
barriers pursuant to waiver decisions, but not in whatever segment of the U.S-Mexico
border currently has the lowest rates of illegal entry.  See App., infra, 214a.  Such a
limitation would be self-defeating; any segment where the Secretary is not permitted
to build would soon become a funnel point for illegal alien crossings that are thwarted
by barriers elsewhere.  See App., infra, 226a; pp. 28-29, infra (further discussing such
implications).  Not only did Congress not plausibly intend that backwards result;
Congress mandated the opposite, directing DHS “to achieve and maintain operational
control over the entire international land  * * *  border[ ] of the United States”—not
just part of it.  Secure Fence Act of 2006 § 2(a), 120 Stat. 2638 (emphasis added).
Ultimately, these interpretive issues are beside the point.  Congress left policy
questions about the appropriate and necessary placement of border barriers to the

24
Secretary, not to the judiciary.  Congress conferred on the Secretary the “sole discre-
tion” to determine whether a waiver is necessary to expeditiously build barriers un-
der IIRIRA Section 102.  IIRIRA § 102(c)(1).  And Congress stripped district courts of
jurisdiction over all non-constitutional challenges to a Secretary’s waiver decision.
The district court transgressed those limits on its authority by adjudicating a statu-
tory challenge that it had no jurisdiction to resolve and then rejecting the Secretary’s
judgment about where border barriers are needed in favor of its own contrary assess-
ment.  That judgment is well beyond the judicial ken—and right in the heartland of
the Secretary’s authority and competence.  The government is overwhelmingly likely
to succeed on the merits.
II.
THE REMAINING FACTORS SUPPORT A STAY
In evaluating a stay application, this Court also considers the applicant’s like-
lihood of obtaining certiorari; its likelihood of suffering irreparable harm; and, in close
cases, the balance of the equities.  See Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190.  Those factors
all support a stay here.
A.
The Court Would Likely Grant Certiorari
Under Section 102’s unusual review scheme, the district court’s unlawful in-
junction “may be reviewed only upon petition for a writ of certiorari to” this Court.
IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(C).  The Court is likely to grant such a petition here because the
decision below conflicts with decisions of this Court in an unprecedented way that
will have severely disruptive consequences, and the government has no other avenue
of appellate review.
The decision below is an extreme outlier.  As explained above (at 8-9), Secre-
taries for over 20 years have been relying on their waiver authority under Section
102(c) to secure the Nation’s borders.  Until now, no court has ever sustained a chal-

25
lenge to the substance of a Secretary’s waiver decision.  On the contrary, courts have
consistently declined to hear non-constitutional challenges to waiver decisions and
have rejected constitutional challenges to the Secretary’s waiver authority.  See p. 9
n.4, supra (collecting cases).5  In Center for Biological Diversity, then-Judge Jackson
declined to hear an ultra vires challenge to a Secretary’s waiver decision in light of
IIRIRA’s jurisdiction-stripping provision, then rejected the remaining constitutional
challenges.  404 F. Supp. 3d. at 237.  The district court in this case, by contrast, cir-
cumvented the limits on its jurisdiction and then misapplied IIRIRA’s text.
Further, the decision below would thwart border-wall construction along a ma-
jor portion of the southwest border in a highly disruptive way—the kind of significant
consequences that heighten the likelihood of this Court’s review.  If the decision below
is left to stand, the Secretary’s waiver authority will be subject to inconsistent legal
regimes along the Nation’s border.  Along most of the border, the Secretary can exer-
cise his waiver authority to expedite barrier construction in areas that he finds to
have high rates of illegal entry.  But under the decision below, the Secretary lacks
that authority along hundreds of miles of the border in the Big Bend Sector.  That
inconsistency is untenable.  If the Secretary cannot fully exercise his authority to
build adequate border-security infrastructure in certain segments, they will quickly
become “funnel points” for illegal alien crossings and the smuggling of contraband.
See App., infra, 226a; pp. 28-29, infra (further discussing this consequence of the in-
junction).  The practical significance of the decision below for the government’s efforts
5  In Zapata County v. Biden, No. 20-cv-106, 2023 WL 11915719 (S.D. Tex. Mar.
31, 2023), a court denied the government’s motion to dismiss claims that a waiver
was unconstitutional and ultra vires on the grounds that the Secretary who issued
the decision was unlawfully appointed.  Those claims did not concern the substance
of the waiver, and the court emphasized that the ultra vires claim was “not directly
assailing a DHS section 102(c) waiver determination” but rather the Secretary’s ap-
pointment.  Id. at *21 (brackets and internal quotation marks omitted).

26
to stem the tide of illegal border crossings and drug trafficking thus counsels strongly
in favor of further review.
Additionally, the district court’s decision “conflicts with relevant decisions of
this Court.”  Sup. Ct. R. 10(c).  The decision below misconstrues this Court’s major-
questions precedents, which clearly apply that doctrine to evaluate alleged statutory
violations rather than alleged constitutional violations.  See pp. 14-19, supra.  And it
conflicts with this Court’s decision in Dalton distinguishing between claims that an
executive officer acted “in excess of his statutory authority” and claims alleging a
“violation of the Constitution.”  511 U.S. at 472.
B.
The Government Will Suffer Irreparable Harm Absent A Stay
1.
The district court’s order irreparably harms the government and the
public by blocking the Secretary’s exercise of his statutorily conferred power to waive
applicable laws as he “determines necessary to ensure expeditious construction” of
border barriers under IIRIRA Section 102.  § 102(c)(1).  When the government is en-
joined from carrying out its responsibilities under a “statute[ ] enacted by represent-
atives of [the] people, it suffers a form of irreparable injury.”  Trump v. CASA, Inc.,
606 U.S. 831, 861 (2025) (citation omitted); see Trump v. California, No. 26A124 (Aug.
24, 2026), slip op. 8-9  (per curiam) (finding that the government was “likely to suffer
irreparable harm” from an injunction that “deal[t] ‘a serious setback’ to the Execu-
tive’s ‘goals’ ”) (citation omitted); DHS v. League of Women Voters, No. 26A308 (Sept.
25, 2026), slip op. 5 (per curiam) (finding that the government was “likely to suffer
irreparable harm” from an order that “set aside” a federal program).  Even the district
court, in denying a stay, correctly found that “because they will continue to be pre-
vented from effectuating their policies, [applicants] have demonstrated that they will
experience at least some degree of irreparable harm absent a stay.”  App., infra, 221a.

27
The government’s injury is particularly pronounced in cases implicating the
government’s “compelling interests in safety and in the integrity of our borders.”  Na-
tional Treasury Emps. Union v. Von Raab, 489 U.S. 656, 672 (1989); see Trump v.
Sierra Club, 588 U.S. 930, 930-931 (2019) (granting a stay of a preliminary injunction
prohibiting border-wall construction).  Congress specifically enacted Section 102(c)’s
waiver provision, and its accompanying limits on judicial review, in order to “ensure
expeditious construction” of border walls and roads without undue interference.
IIRIRA § 102(c)(1); see Conf. Rep. 172 (describing Conferees’ “intent to ensure that
judicial review of actions or decisions of the Secretary not delay the expeditious con-
struction of border security infrastructure”).  Now, the district court’s injunction sig-
nificantly frustrates the government’s ability to stop the flow of illegal aliens and
drugs across the southern border.  The Secretary identified the Big Bend project areas
at issue because of the high rates of illegal-alien crossings and drug smuggling in the
region over the past several years.  See App., infra, 2a, 4a, 7a.  Between fiscal year
2021 and fiscal year 2025, U.S. Border Patrol apprehended over 89,000 illegal aliens
attempting to enter through the Big Bend Sector and seized over 87,574 pounds of
marijuana, over 867 pounds of cocaine, over 1156 pounds of methamphetamine, over
12 pounds of heroin, and over 94 pounds of fentanyl.  See First Enriquez Decl. ¶ 42;
App., infra, 223a.  During fiscal years 2021 and 2022, unlawful entries spiked to rec-
ord highs of over 30,000 annual encounters in the Big Bend Sector.  See App., infra,
21a, 24a-25a.  Meanwhile, the quantity of illegal drugs seized in the Big Bend Sector
in fiscal year 2026 surpassed the annual totals for each of the previous three fiscal
years.  See id. at 10a-16a, 18a.  And those numbers do not even account for the aliens
and smugglers who successfully crossed the border undetected.  Id. at 227a.

28
The record illustrates the need for additional border-security infrastructure in
the area, which transnational criminal organizations have thus far been able to ex-
ploit.  See App., infra, 227a-228a.  Specifically, the Sinaloa and Juarez cartels operate
on the Mexican side of the border south of the Big Bend Sector and engage in a range
of dangerous activity from human smuggling to the trafficking of drugs and weapons
around the Big Bend region.  Id. at 227a.  In August 2022, for example, Border Patrol
agents executing a search warrant at a ranch house in Van Horn, Texas seized about
13,000 pounds of marijuana that was confirmed to have crossed the border without
detection in the Big Bend Sector.  Id. at 228a.  And in August 2023, Border Patrol
agents in Texas apprehended the leader of the Juarez Cartel of Ojinaga, Mexico, who
admitted that he had illegally entered the United States by wading the Rio Grande
River in the Big Bend region.  Ibid.
Even with the additional enforcement tools and resources available to CBP
since January 2025, Big Bend’s landscape makes it difficult to police, and aliens have
succeeded in illegally crossing the border in the Big Bend Sector and causing harm
inside the United States.  App., infra, 228a.  Several recent examples of illegal entries
in the Big Bend Sector illustrate those dangers.  In May 2026, for example, an alien
illegally entered the United States on foot in the Big Bend Sector, stole a car, then
drove to a Texas school with young children inside, which he attempted to enter while
armed with a high-powered firearm.  Id. at 229a.  Law enforcement pursued the sus-
pect, resulting in a chase and a deadly shootout.  Ibid.  In June 2026, three cartel
recruits were apprehended in the Big Bend Sector after crossing the border illegally
with firearms.  Id. at 230a-231a.  And in September 2026, three individuals were
apprehended in Big Bend National Park as they attempted to engage in human smug-
gling.  Id. at 231a-232a.

29
The Secretary has determined that border barriers are necessary to safeguard
the border against such infiltration.  App., infra, 2a, 4a, 7a; see id. at 232a.  DHS has
further determined that leaving an open segment of the border without barriers in
the Big Bend region would create a funnel point for illegal-alien crossings and smug-
glers.  Id. at 226a.  That conclusion makes sense:  Bad actors who might otherwise
have crossed the border at a different entry point are likely to target and exploit gaps
in the border’s barriers where they find them.  As the record illustrates, the Big Bend
region is vulnerable to such exploitation, notwithstanding its rugged character.
Thus, in CBP’s view, “not having a border barrier system in this particular area would
make it a vulnerable and desirable area” for cartels “to operate along the southwest
border.”  Id. at 227a.
The district court’s injunction exposes the United States to those dangers.  The
court stayed the effectiveness of the Big Bend waivers and enjoined applicants from
building any “border barrier or related infrastructure,” in the Big Bend Sector “until
and unless” applicants “comply with all applicable laws.”  App., infra, 202a.  Expedi-
tious compliance with all laws waived by the Secretary—such as NEPA, the Endan-
gered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, Pub. L. No. 89-665, 80 Stat.
915 (1966), and others—is not feasible. NEPA’s procedures alone have historically
imposed “[d]elay upon delay,” Seven County Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle County, 605
U.S. 168, 184 (2025), and still remain time-consuming.  See 42 U.S.C. 4336a(g)(1)(A)
(Supp. V 2023) (requiring that environmental impact statements under NEPA must
be completed within “2 years”).  So in practice, the district court’s order effectively
halts border-barrier construction altogether in the Big Bend Sector pending the res-
olution of this litigation.  As explained above, DHS and CBP anticipate an increase
in illegal immigration and drug smuggling across the United States border without a

30
border barrier in the Big Bend Sector.  App., infra, 232a.  If left to stand, the injunc-
tion thus will impede the government’s “compelling” interest in protecting “the integ-
rity of our borders.”  Von Raab, 489 U.S. at 672.
2.
Beyond those border-security harms, the government faces irreparable
operational and financial injuries if the injunction remains in place during this
Court’s review.  The government has awarded contracts for five border-barrier con-
struction projects in the project areas covered by the Big Bend waivers.  App., infra,
220a.  Before the injunction issued, the contractors and their employees had been
working on a range of pre-construction and construction activities.  See id. at 222a-
223a.  For one of the projects, field personnel had already been deployed and were
working 60 hours per week, and heavy equipment had been mobilized to facilitate
construction.  Id. at 221a-222a.  Workers there had already constructed about three-
quarters of a mile of border barrier, and temporary field offices, supply yards, a water-
delivery system, and a temporary concrete batch plant had been installed.  Ibid.
Given the scale of that effort, the injunction imposes significant operational costs on
the government, its contractors, and workers.  Ibid.
Every day that the injunction remains in effect and construction work is sus-
pended, the government’s contractors will continue to incur financial liabilities.  Even
while work is suspended, contractors still need to pay for land leases, offices, and the
security necessary to protect equipment and materials from theft while they are not
in use, among other expenses.  App., infra, 222a.  CBP estimates that those suspen-
sion costs will total over $460,000 per day.  Ibid.  The government remains responsi-
ble for reimbursing such costs, which it will have to pay from funds that it would
otherwise spend on actual border-barrier construction.  Ibid.  If the injunction is later
lifted and construction permitted to continue, the government may also be required

31
to pay the contractors “acceleration costs” in order to maintain the original project
schedules.  Ibid.  These costs cannot be recouped if the government prevails at the
end of the litigation.  Ibid.  They, too, support a stay in this case.
3.
The district court did not even address the government’s compelling bor-
der-security interests or its operational concerns in its order granting the injunction
or its subsequent opinion.  See App., infra, 202a, 217a.  Instead, it dismissed the
government’s harms in a single sentence, asserting that “if enjoined,” the government
will “only suffer a temporary delay while [the district court] assesses the merits of
the pending summary judgment motions.”  Id. at 217a.  In its opinion denying a stay,
the court at least acknowledged that the government “will experience at least some
degree of irreparable harm,” but continued to minimize that harm as mere “ ‘tempo-
rary delay.’ ”  Id. at 236a (citation omitted).  Left unexamined are the consequences
of that “temporary delay”:  diminished border protections in an area of high illegal
entry and drug trafficking, plus significant operational and financial costs.  The
court’s failure to afford “[a] proper consideration” of the government’s important in-
terests, Winter v. NRDC, 555 U.S. 7, 23 (2008), renders the injunction improper and
underscores the need for a stay.  See National Park Serv. v. National Trust for His-
toric Pres. in the U.S., No. 26A203 (Aug. 31, 2026), slip op. 7-8 (per curiam).
C.
The Balance Of Equities Favors A Stay
Because this is not a close case, the Court need not balance the equities.  See
Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190.  But if it does, the government’s compelling border-
security and operational interests vastly outweigh any aesthetic, recreational, or cul-
tural injuries that respondents may suffer if the Secretary’s waiver decisions take
effect.  This Court has already balanced similar equities in the government’s favor

32
when it granted a stay of a district court’s preliminary injunction prohibiting border-
wall construction in Sierra Club, 588 U.S. at 930.  The same balance applies here.
1.
The primary harm asserted by respondents is that the construction in
the Big Bend region will affect “their enjoyment of the wild spaces in the Big Bend
Sector.”  App., infra, 216a.  Those subjective, attenuated injuries cannot justify an
injunction of the Secretary’s waiver decisions.  Congress’s enactment of Section
102(c)—which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-
protection laws—reflects an explicit preference for expeditious border construction
over the very harms that respondents assert.  See IIRIRA § 102(c)(1).  A court decid-
ing whether to issue an injunction cannot disregard that legislative “order of priori-
ties.”  TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153, 194 (1978); see United States v. Oakland Cannabis
Buyers’ Coop., 532 U.S. 483, 497 (2001) (“Courts of equity cannot, in their discretion,
reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute.”).  The environmental inter-
ests that Congress permitted the Secretary to subordinate in order to facilitate expe-
ditious border-barrier construction cannot justify enjoining such construction.
This Court, too, has already determined that recreational and aesthetic inju-
ries like the ones asserted by respondents are insufficient to justify enjoining the con-
struction of a border wall.  In Trump v. Sierra Club, the plaintiffs similarly contended
that construction at the border would harm their ability to fish, hike, and camp.  See
Gov’t Appl. at 38, Sierra Club, supra (No. 19A60).  The Court granted a stay of district
court’s preliminary injunction, Sierra Club, 588 U.S. at 930, necessarily determining
that the plaintiffs’ asserted injuries were outweighed by the government’s compelling
interest in border security.
The Court has also found a plaintiff ’s asserted aesthetic injuries insufficient to
support a preliminary injunction in contexts beyond the border wall.  In National

33
Park Service, for example, the Court held that “the offense” that a plaintiff ’s member
“will suffer from having to view” the renovated East Wing of the White House is out-
weighed by the “national security and other harms that would likely arise” for the
government from enjoining its construction.  Slip op. 6-7.  And in Winter, 555 U.S. at
25-26, the Court vacated a preliminary injunction after determining that the plain-
tiffs’ interests in “observ[ing],” “photograph[ing],” and “conduct[ing] scientific re-
search” on marine mammals were “plainly outweigh[ed]” by the Navy’s operational
needs.  The equities in this case cut the same way.
2.
In all events, the record shows that any harms to respondents from stay-
ing the injunction will be minimal.  Again, respondents are primarily concerned with
preserving their ability to enjoy the Big Bend wilderness.  But the record shows that
the construction planned for Big Bend’s public recreational areas is limited.  CBP has
explained that no border-barrier construction whatsoever is planned inside Big Bend
Ranch State Park.  D. Ct. Doc. 60-1, ¶ 22 (Sept. 9, 2026) (Second Enriquez Decl.).  And
in Big Bend National Park, the only planned barrier construction is a 17-mile non-
contiguous vehicle barrier system that “should have little to no impact” on the “pub-
lic’s ability to access” the park or the Rio Grande River.  First Enriquez Decl. ¶ 34.
Although CBP plans to construct a 30-foot pedestrian barrier in other areas of the
Big Bend Sector, it has disclaimed any intent to construct such a barrier in the state
or national park.  See CBP, Statement from CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott cor-
recting the record on Big Bend border security projects (Aug. 13, 2026),
https://perma.cc/XW22-HTQJ (“We are NOT building a 30-foot wall or stadium light-
ing through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park or the Black Gap
Wildlife Management Area.”).

34
In other words, most of the planned construction will not occur in state or na-
tional park land, but rather on privately owned land for which CBP will secure a
private right of access.  See First Enriquez Decl. ¶ 26.  Respondents have no compel-
ling interest in preserving the “scenic character” of other people’s private property.
P.I. Mot. 17.  And to the extent that border barriers will be constructed on land owned
by a respondent, CBP has a long history of working with landowners to mitigate the
impacts of construction through a variety of accommodations.  See Second Enriquez
Decl. ¶ 19.  Respondents’ speculative complaints that construction could harm a his-
toric adobe church on the opposite side of the highway from planned barriers, see
App., infra, 130a, are likewise unsupported by evidence.  In all events, the record
shows that CBP is taking numerous steps to minimize the risk of the very environ-
mental harms that respondents allege, such as using infrared illuminators instead of
stadium lighting in rural areas to minimize light pollution in Big Bend’s dark skies,
and conducting biological surveys of all project areas to identify plant and animal
species for preservation.  First Enriquez Decl. ¶¶ 36-40.
The district court mentioned none of those efforts, instead finding that the bal-
ance of harms favored respondents because construction of waterborne barriers in
the Rio Grande River would “restrict” the “livelihood” of plaintiff river guides.  App.,
infra, 215a.  But CBP’s planned construction does not include waterborne barriers
and will have little to no impact on the public’s ability to access the Rio Grande River
in Big Bend National Park.  See First Enriquez Decl. ¶¶ 9, 18-20, 22, 34-35; Second
Enriquez Decl. ¶¶ 17, 22.  The court also found that construction could affect the
livelihood of a local rancher by cutting off irrigation to his crops, App., infra, 215a,
but neglected to mention CBP’s practice of consulting with landowners regarding ex-
isting irrigation lines before construction, Second Enriquez Decl. ¶ 19.  True, the court

35
apparently determined that construction in the Big Bend Sector would harm wildlife
based on anecdotal reports of increased roadkill from construction vehicles, see App.,
infra, 216a.  But when a court elevates alleged harms like an anecdotal increase in
roadkill over the very real and far-reaching consequences of halting all construction
across hundreds of miles of the southern border and thwarting the government’s bor-
der-security efforts, the balance of equities has gone unacceptably awry.  This Court
should stay the district court’s unlawful injunction.
III.
THE COURT
SHOULD
GRANT
CERTIORARI
AND
SUMMARILY
REVERSE
In addition to granting a stay, this Court should construe this application as a
petition for a writ of certiorari, grant the petition, and summarily reverse.  See Wis-
consin Legislature v. Wisconsin Elections Comm’n, 595 U.S. 398, 401 (2022) (per cu-
riam) (granting similar request).  In certain cases, “the error in the lower court’s de-
cision is so obvious” that the appropriate course of action is to “grant certiorari and
simultaneously reverse.”  Stephen M. Shapiro et al., Supreme Court Practice § 4.17,
at 280 (10th ed. 2013); see, e.g., Doe v. Dynamic Physical Therapy, LLC, 607 U.S. 11,
11 (2025) (per curiam) (summarily reversing “incorrect” decision); Margolin v. Na-
tional Ass’n of Immigration Judges, 608 U.S. 339, 343 (2026) (per curiam) (summarily
reversing decision that  “violated the party-presentation principle”).  This case man-
ifestly fits that bill.  The district court found jurisdiction by flagrantly misreading
this Court’s major-questions precedents; proceeded to find a major-questions problem
where none exists; then rewrote IIRIRA to hamstring the Secretary’s waiver analysis.
Those errors are so obvious that this Court can swiftly correct them on the merits
without further briefing or oral argument.

36
Summary reversal would be particularly appropriate to quickly put to rest any
doubt over the scope of the Secretary’s waiver authority under IIRIRA Section 102(c).
The Secretary regularly relies on Section 102(c)’s waiver authority to expeditiously
construct border barriers across the southern border, not only in the Big Bend Sector.
See, e.g., 91 Fed. Reg. 62,739 (Oct. 2, 2026) (IIRIRA waiver decision for a project area
in New Mexico).  Summarily reversing the district court’s order in this case will pre-
vent other courts from repeating its errors and entertaining statutory challenges to
Section 102(c) waivers that they lack jurisdiction to consider.
CONCLUSION
This Court should stay the order of the United States District Court for the
Western District of Texas.  The Court should also construe this application as a peti-
tion for a writ of certiorari, grant the petition, and summarily reverse the district
court’s order.
Respectfully submitted.
